candidates.title: Technology Micron Pauses Work on $4.5 Billion Taiwan Plant After Labor Spat
candidates.summary: Micron Pauses Work on $4.5 Billion Taiwan Plant After Labor Spat Micron Technology Inc. has suspended plans for a memory chip plant in Taiwan due to a labor dispute, throwing into question the fate of a major production base for crucial AI components. The company has halted construction of a plant
candidates.full: Micron Pauses Work on $4.5 Billion Taiwan Plant After Labor Spat Micron Technology Inc. has suspended plans for a memory chip plant in Taiwan due to a labor dispute, throwing into question the fate of a major production base for crucial AI components. The company has halted construction of a plant in the northern Taiwanese city of Taoyuan, citing mounting uncertainties, including the risk that an agreement with a local labor union will get overturned. The suspension raises the possibility Micron will reconsider plans for its broader manufacturing hub in Taiwan, which helps it compete with other companies, and would be a major blow to the island if the company scaled back there. Micron Technology Inc. has suspended plans for a memory chip plant in Taiwan due to a protracted labor dispute, according to people familiar with the matter, throwing into question the fate of a major production base for crucial AI components. The US company has all but halted construction of a plant in the northern Taiwanese city of Taoyuan, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the deliberations are private. Executives are concerned about mounting uncertainties, including the risk that an agreement with a local labor union will get overturned. Micron has informed Taiwanese officials and a supplier about its plans to suspend construction in the city, the people said. The company’s shares slid as much as 7.3% in US trading. Tensions between Micron and its workers flared this year after employees demanded higher compensation, seeking more of the record profits generated from the AI build-out. The potential disruption to Micron’s plans in Taiwan — an island that produces three-fifths of the US firm’s conventional chips — threatens to further cloud a market already grappling with endemic shortages of memory. Micron — which has invested close to $50 billion in Taiwan over three decades — had planned on making high-bandwidth memory and DRAM at the new Taoyuan plant using top-end equipment from ASML Holding NV. While it isn’t considered a giant facility by modern standards, those components are intertwined with Nvidia Corp. accelerators and the global AI data center boom, and in such short supply that prices are skyrocketing. “Taiwan plays an important role in Micron’s global footprint, and our operations today continue as normal,” Micron said in a statement, without addressing questions about the Taoyuan complex. “We are confident in maintaining business continuity for our customers.” Read More: Micron Gives Taiwan Staff $32,000 Bonus After Profits Soar Micron secured a deal with the bigger of its two unions in October, but the company may need to renegotiate because some employees are balking at the terms, according to the people. The suspension raises the possibility Micron will reconsider plans for its broader manufacturing hub in Taiwan, which helps it compete with South Korea’s Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc., and China’s CXMT Corp. Micron had budgeted $3 billion to $4.5 billion toward the Taoyuan complex, which included purchases of ASML gear, one of the people said. There’s still some minor work being done on the site to ensure its safety, but construction will freeze after that, the people added. Dubbed Fab 11E, it was previously scheduled to come online in 2028. Micron is Taiwan’s largest foreign investor, and it would be a major blow to the island if the company scaled back there. Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs didn’t comment on Micron’s move to pause some expansion, but said the government was helping the company implement investment plans. “The government supports the legal agreement the company has reached with the union, and will shoulder and share responsibilities with the local government to help resolve the differences and create a win-win outcome,” the ministry said in a statement to Bloomberg News. The Taoyuan government said it hasn’t been notified of a suspension, though it’s hoping Micron and its employees can reach a consensus. Taiwan Suspects China Behind Brief Pakistan Airspace Ban Taiwan’s Envoy Prods Trump Administration on Arms Sale Trump Says Xi Knows ‘How I Feel’ on Taiwan After Summit China Tells Japanese Lawmakers Taiwan Is at Heart of Tensions Taiwan’s economy and stock market have gotten a boost from the AI boom, with the likes of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. building plants at an unprecedented pace. Yet its viability as a long-term investment destination is at risk from potential Chinese military intervention. Even as Micron considers slowing down in Taiwan, it’s racing to ready factories elsewhere. It’s committed to investing $250 billion in US manufacturing, including in New York state. It has also been expanding in Japan and Singapore. Read More: Huge AI Bonuses in Korea Spark Debate Over Sharing Tech Wealth The Taoyuan plant isn’t the largest for Micron in Taiwan. But it’s a showpiece project for a US company with an outsized local presence. Taiwan currently accounts for 60% of Micron’s global output of DRAM or dynamic random access chips, the common form of memory used in computers and phones. The area also produces a big chunk of its high-bandwidth memory or HBM, which is used in AI systems. The island is Micron’s largest site in terms of personnel, with 15,000 employees or about a quarter of the company’s total. The Taoyuan union represents fewer than 3,000, with the bulk of the remainder joining the far larger Taichung body. The Taoyuan group has demanded Micron distribute 15% of its operating profit to global employees, because Samsung and SK Hynix have adopted similar measures. Union Chair Jerry Lin said the employees also want all-cash incentives, rather than partially in stock. Read More: Micron Gives Bullish Forecast, Even as Pay Raises Crimp Margins The union is now trying to form a bigger group by recruiting members from the Taichung body — to help try and annul the existing pact. It will then demand Micron restart negotiations, Lin said. While Micron hasn’t disclosed terms of the standing deal, Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs said the agreement would lift junior engineers’ annual packages by more than two-fold to NT$4 million ($121,450), on average. Senior engineers would get a three-fold bump to NT$6 million. The mean annual pay for an engineer at listed local semiconductor firms was NT$2.58 million in 2025, according to employment site 104 Job Bank. Micron felt confident the agreement reached with the larger union was legally binding, according to a person familiar with the matter. Taichung union Chair Mark Hsu also acknowledged its legality, but said he respected the move by its smaller peer to form a bigger organization. Talks with the Taoyuan union are ongoing. “We look forward to reaching an agreement,” Micron said. — With assistance from Dong Lyu (Updates with trading from third paragraph) Morgan Stanley Offers $2.3 Billion Debt for Dell Family Deal S&P 500 Sinks 4% as AI Washout Rattles Wall Street: Markets Wrap ING Said to Be Seller of $500 Million Data Center Loan Portfolio Goldman Traders’ Phones Blow Up With Investors Seeking Answers to AI Rout DeSantis Calls GOP Midterm Wipeout ‘Extinction Level Event’

candidates.title: Palantir mines battlefield intelligence but is Ukraine 'paying with blood'? | Technology News
candidates.summary: Palantir harvests battlefield data that Ukraine pays for ‘with blood’ The US company is using Kyiv’s unique war data to train its controversial technologies. Months into Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Palantir’s CEO Alex Karp became the first chief of a major Western Big Tech company to pe
candidates.full: Palantir harvests battlefield data that Ukraine pays for ‘with blood’ The US company is using Kyiv’s unique war data to train its controversial technologies. Months into Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Palantir’s CEO Alex Karp became the first chief of a major Western Big Tech company to personally visit Kyiv. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in June 2022 that he was “delighted” to receive the support of such a company in the fight against Russia “on the digital front line”. The Florida-based software development firm’s partnership has paid off. Ukraine has since become the first nation in modern history to systematically collect battlefield data, a crucial asset for training military artificial intelligence (AI) to recognise patterns and make predictions. The trove of real-world combat data obtained from video and sensor feeds over four years of conflict is helping Ukraine monitor, predict and respond to Russian attacks with the help of Palantir’s products. Yet observers say the data is also boosting the capabilities of the United States corporation whose technologies are implicated in human rights abuses, including in Israel’s genocide in Gaza, raising questions about the growing leverage that private tech corporations are acquiring over sovereign states. A ‘strategic advantage’ Palantir was founded in the aftermath of the 2001 attack on New York’s World Trade Center to help the US defence industry build a single data environment from which to monitor and respond to incoming threats. To reflect such a mission, the company was named after a stone in JRR Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings that grants powers that border on omniscience. Yasir Atalan, deputy director of the Futures Lab at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said Palantir makes “different forms of data talk to each other”. In the military context, data from missiles, radars, the automatic identification system (AIS) and open sources is gathered on one screen, offering a “larger view of the battlefield”, Atalan said. Similar solutions are available to governments for civil purposes, including border control, health services, tax and revenue – and mass surveillance. With more data, systems use statistical learning to recognise patterns to make accurate predictions, enabling military systems to make split-second, automated tactical decisions. Under this premise, large datasets based on real-life scenarios are coveted by companies aiming to outperform their competitors. “Good battlefield data is extremely rare and hard to come by,” Elke Schwarz, a lecturer focusing on digital technologies at Queen Mary University of London, told Al Jazeera. Because of its scarcity, “those with access to [it] have a strategic advantage”. Data originating from Ukraine may not be directly applicable to another conflict but is still crucial for training, Schwarz said. “Building a system that correctly identifies a tank, for instance, requires a large volume of tank images, ideally in all kinds of weather conditions,” she explained. Similarly, large volumes of behavioural data – information on how people react to a given scenario – are key in tracking, profiling and predicting human activity in mass surveillance systems. Ukraine’s invaluable battlefield data The pinnacle of the collaboration between Palantir and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence came in January with the launch of a specialised software platform, the Brave1 Dataroom, which uses battlefield data to train artificial intelligence for military applications. But prominent figures in Ukraine’s defence sector have questioned their government’s decision to share the country’s valuable asset with a private tech company under undisclosed terms. “Ukraine has something that no other country in the world has,” Valerii Markus, a serviceman and former chief sergeant, wrote on Facebook. “We are paying with blood for data that someone else can convert into capital, international influence, and big money.” The company maintains it does not acquire customer data. In an emailed statement to Al Jazeera, it said that “customers own and control their data”. Palantir’s software helps them “integrate and analyse their existing data sets,” the company said, adding: “Palantir never uses or retains customer data for its own purposes.” Schwarz, at Queen Mary University London, said Palantir does not need to possess the data to benefit from it. “Rather, it works with the data that is made available,” she said. Civil liberties and data protection Palantir’s technologies, contracted by private clients and government agencies around the world, are known to have been implicated in human rights abuses. Its core software platforms, ICM and FALCON, facilitated the administration of US President Donald Trump in detaining and deporting thousands of people, including asylum seekers, since January 2025. Amnesty International found the company aggregated massive amounts of data, built detailed individual profiles to track migrants and asylum seekers and assisted with deportations, contrary to its obligations to avoid causing or contributing to human rights abuses under international law. The company has also assisted Israel in its war in Gaza, which a United Nations inquiry found bears the hallmarks of genocide. Last year, UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese found “reasonable grounds” to believe Palantir provided AI platforms used for battlefield data integration and automated decision-making in the war that has killed more than 74,500 Palestinians since October 2023. In the United Kingdom, the National Health Service (NHS), police, military and local councils all signed multimillion-pound contracts with Palantir to integrate user data, but the agreements have been met with public backlash. Nonprofit organisation Corporate Accountability launched a campaign against the 330-million-pound ($440m) contract between the NHS and Palantir to provide a new data platform. The watchdog warned the company is “at the heart of the dystopian marriage of Big Tech, the surveillance and detention industry, and rising fascism”. Palantir in April published a 22-point summary of Karp’s coauthored book on X, which was widely criticised for promoting an authoritarian, antidemocratic worldview by questioning the efficacy of liberal democracy and arguing that some cultures produce vital advances while others are regressive. Fatimah Shaikh, Corporate Accountability’s deputy campaigns director, said, “Palantir is not a corporation we can trust” to hold British citizens’ sensitive personal information. “We should all be able to get medical care without fearing for our safety or privacy,” she told Al Jazeera. Ilia Siatitsa, senior legal officer at Privacy International in the UK, said tech companies like Palantir blur the line between military and civil applications. They are also opaque about how they use customers’ data by virtue of their involvement in national security, she added. Siatitsa argued the company could potentially use personal information to train its products – including those with a military application – without explicit consent from the users. “If my data is going to be feeding into a war machine, I want to know about it,” she said. “I need to have the choice, not only [as a matter of] privacy, but also from an ethical point of view.” In June, Britain announced it was reviewing the NHS’s data contract with Palantir after parliamentary pressure. Growing dependencies Private tech companies are supporting military and civil infrastructure, to the point where governments may become reliant on them to conduct military operations or run national services, experts say. Anna Nadibaidze, researcher at the Center for War Studies at the University of Southern Denmark, said the balance of power has been shifting. “We’re used to state armies, nations’ armies being the main players,” Nadibaidze said, adding that now those players are reliant on products supplied by the private sector. “So what if they choose to not supply this infrastructure any more?” She argued Elon Musk’s SpaceX offered a valid example. Ukraine has come to rely heavily on the company’s Starlink satellites for communications on the battlefield and effective warfare, but in late September 2022, during a pivotal push by Ukraine to retake Kherson from Russia, the tech billionaire suddenly provoked a communications blackout. Amid tensions between Washington and Europe, several countries are now refraining from using Palantir’s products. France’s Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu in June said domestic intelligence services would ditch Palantir’s products in an effort to avoid “strategic dependency”. Germany’s military also said it would no longer use the company’s products. Spanish publication El Confidencial revealed in July that Spanish authorities quietly instructed state-backed companies to avoid signing new contracts with Palantir, citing concerns that sensitive national security information could be exposed. Palantir’s reliability as a partner has also been called into question in Ukraine after the company finalised in September a strategic partnership with Nebius, a Dutch company founded as an offshoot of Russian technology giant Yandex. Denys Shtilerman, chief designer and co-owner of Fire Point, a Ukrainian defence-tech company that develops and produces UAV and missile systems, said “the very same Palantir that works with Ukrainian combat data” had struck a deal with Yandex cofounder Arkady Volozh. Volozh’s description of Russia’s war as “barbaric” has not eased Shtilerman’s concerns. “Our combat data is not free raw material for Western technology corporations. It is a strategic asset of the state,” he wrote on X in a response to Kyiv’s collaboration with Palantir. “Ukraine has paid for it with blood. We have no right to simply hand over the most valuable asset we possess.”

candidates.title: How the College Board Is Fighting A.I. Cheating on the SAT Tests - The New York Times
candidates.summary: Fighting A.I. Cheating on the SAT Is a Cat-and-Mouse Game Priced at $499 and payable by cryptocurrency only, Auto SAT was marketed as a foolproof way to ace the SAT tests. It used artificial intelligence to project answers onto a student’s computer screen — during the test. But as soon as Auto SA
candidates.full: Fighting A.I. Cheating on the SAT Is a Cat-and-Mouse Game Priced at $499 and payable by cryptocurrency only, Auto SAT was marketed as a foolproof way to ace the SAT tests. It used artificial intelligence to project answers onto a student’s computer screen — during the test. But as soon as Auto SAT went on sale in March, the College Board, which sponsors the SAT tests, discovered it on social media. The organization purchased a copy of Auto SAT, evaluated it and then pushed design and code changes to its test to thwart Auto SAT’s effectiveness. It filed a lawsuit against the malware developer and demanded that the website be taken down. The College Board’s efforts against Auto SAT are among the latest moves in what has become a costly cat-and-mouse game against global cyberintrusions. Cheating operations taking advantage of advances in A.I. technology are forcing the $2 billion nonprofit to step up its defenses. The SAT tests went online in 2024, a move aimed partly at ending test leaks. But, looking to capitalize on consumer demand for high scores, scammers have devised a medley of tricks to undermine the security of the digital test. They often combine sophisticated A.I. tools and a pervasive form of cheating involving time zones. Test takers in New Zealand, for example, can log in hours before others around the world, copy questions and then sell them in later time zones. Students, tutors and others have raised alarms, and the College Board has responded. To thwart “time zone cheating,” the College Board is planning to put in place a new SAT testing schedule sometime in 2027, according to Massie Ritsch, a spokesman for the organization. The new schedule has not yet been announced, but it will eliminate the hourslong gap between tests given in different time zones, reducing the possibility of time zone cheating. A similar plan was announced by the College Board in July for the organization’s Advanced Placement tests. And in other security moves, the College Board has banned wearable A.I. smart glasses and started tracking keystrokes and cursor movements in some locations. The security efforts come after students and others have sent complaints to the College Board about SAT test security, in emails obtained by The New York Times. They pointed to SAT test questions that have appeared on social media, most recently during the October international test. (The test is administered exclusively in English worldwide.) In March, a group of SAT test prep tutors and recent test-takers in Uzbekistan emailed the College Board to report “documented leaks across multiple international administrations,” specifically complaining about test items available on the web platform Telegram five hours before the test started in Central Asia. In an Oct. 12 email to the College Board, shared with The Times, a tutor who asked to be anonymous to protect his school and students wrote that a leaked test circulated on social media in Europe at 1:30 a.m. the day of the test — hours before students in Europe would take it Camille Thompson, vice president of test security for the College Board, said that despite occasional problems, the organization remained confident that the digital SAT test was generally secure. The digital SAT test is an adaptive exam, meaning that students are asked different questions depending on how well they answer the early questions. The variations minimize the potential for cheating. While the College Board will not disclose the exact number of possible variations of the test, the nonprofit says that tests vary considerably from “region to region around the globe, but also from computer to computer.” Ms. Thompson said that the percentage of high scores remained the same, another indication that the test was still secure. “We haven’t seen a significant drift in test takers who are receiving scores at the upper end of the scoring system,” she said in an interview. Other incidents, though, have also raised concerns. In a separate instance of potential cheating in Uzbekistan, the authorities in Tashkent, the nation’s capital, arrested several men this fall, accusing them of operating a high-tech SAT test cheating operation. And October versions of the test, which some tutors said contained authentic questions, appeared on a website called bluebooky.com. The website had more than 500,000 page views in August and collects fees from users. Its name is a knockoff of the College Board’s official test app, Bluebook. Bluebooky, which did not respond to an emailed request for comment, recently changed its URL to bluecorn.org, after another similar site, called bluebookplus.com, was shut down by the College Board. Provided a copy of the October test questions available on bluebooky.com, the College Board would not comment on their authenticity. Auto SAT, the app identified by the College Board in March, used malware to bypass the lockdown screen on the SAT exam site, according to the College Board’s lawsuit. The malware could then access SAT test questions in real time and send them to an A.I. chatbot, which displayed the answers on a student’s computer during test administration. A small dot would appear on a student’s screen to indicate the correct answer to multiple choice questions. The bot also provided answers to free response questions. The malware instructed students to take their time, according to the College Board’s lawsuit. “Do not rush through it and if a proctor is nearby, you can leave your mouse idle and the overlay indicator will disappear until you move your mouse again,” the instructions said. The College Board said it had identified four people who used the malware in March. The nonprofit ultimately ended its lawsuit, partly because it was never able to serve court papers. The SAT test is not the only digital exam vulnerable to security problems. Soon after filing the lawsuit, the College Board said it had detected a time zone cheating scheme during an AP biology test in New Zealand. At an AP conference in July sponsored by the College Board, the head of its AP program, Trevor Packer, said the scheme also employed sophisticated technology. “A student that has malware or some sophisticated A.I. tool on their device is able to harvest those exam questions and, within minutes, begin selling them to students in later time zones,” Dr. Packer said, according to a transcript of his remarks provided by the College Board. When the College Board detected the problem in New Zealand, the day’s AP testing was shut down there and the tests were rescheduled. Partly as a result of that breach, the College Board has already announced a major revamp of its AP tests, which high school students can take to receive college credit. Beginning next year, seven different versions of the tests will be administered, rather than the current three, and tests will be rescheduled in some zones. Test takers in the United States will not see major scheduling changes. ACT Inc., which administers the ACT test and is the SAT test’s biggest competitor, said it was aware of allegations that questions from an exam administered in the United States on Oct. 17 were posted on Telegram before the Oct. 24 international test. Jason Happel, senior vice president for test security, said the organization had not seen any significant impacts, however. Would-be cheaters appear to be growing more brazen. On Oct. 23, bluebooky.com pitched its wares to 5,000 customers on Telegram, telling them to “avoid spending money on third-party sellers who claim to offer early access to the test.” It promised that the questions it offered would be authentic and available before the November SAT test, scheduled for this Saturday. Stephanie Saul reports on colleges and universities, with a recent focus on the dramatic changes in college admissions and the debate around diversity, equity and inclusion in higher education.

candidates.full: Rassvet: sovereignty has an orbital address ️ A country cannot outsource its communications and call itself strategically independent. Russia’s Rassvet programme addresses that problem above the clouds. TASS reports that the constellation uses Russian-developed laser links, with civilian trials already under way. Its purpose is broader than winning a satellite-counting contest with Elon Musk. For Ukraine, the military implication is clear: with suitable terminals and coverage, satellite links could let Russian drone operators receive imagery and adjust missions in flight. That is a potential capability, not proof behind every recent strike. The strategic prize is control over the connection. candidates.full: «А з ким мені зустрічатися?». Фіцо літає приватним літаком на курорт з коханкою та купує дорогу нерухомість — ЗМІ Журналісти дізналися, що Фіцо літає на курорти з молодою юристкою (Фото: Скриншот відео via Бабель) В останні вихідні жовтня прем'єр-міністра Словаччини Роберта Фіцо помітили разом із Катаріною Салайовою, яку називають його коханкою, у Хорватії. Вони прибули туди приватним літаком, а опозиційні депутати підрахували, що протягом останніх чотирьох місяців премʼєр здійснив щонайменше вісім таких перельотів. Їхню загальну вартість оцінюють приблизно у 120 тисяч євро. Про це пише видання Бабель, яке поспілкувалося із журналістом-розслідувачем словацького видання Aktuality.sk Томашем Киселем, який досліджував статки Фіцо та діяльність Салайової. 29 жовтня Фіцо і Салайова ішли летовищем у Братиславі до невеликого приватного літака, яким потім вирушили до хорватського Спліту, недалеко від якого знаходиться приморське місто Ражань — одне з улюблених місць відпочинку премʼєра. Світлини з аеропорту в своїх соцмережах опублікував депутат опозиційної партії Свобода і солідарність (SaS) Алоїз Гліна, додавши до них іронічний підпис, мовляв, прем'єр вирушив на відпочинок «у супроводі своєї законної дружини». Проте офіційною дружиною Фіцо майже 40 років є Світлана Фіцова. Принаймні, про їхнє розлучення публічно не повідомляли, каже Кисель. Колега Гліни по партії, депутатка Мартіна Байо Голечкова, закликала Фіцо оприлюднити рахунок за авіапереліт. За її оцінками, вартість подорожі становила від 8 до 12 тисяч євро. Це приблизно дорівнює місячній зарплаті прем'єр-міністра: за даними Aktuality.sk, у 2026 році Фіцо заробляє близько 10,4 тисячі євро на місяць. «Ніхто мені ніколи нічого не дав задарма», — заявив Фіцо у відеозверненні 31 жовтня. Він додав, що працює чотири десятиліття, багато років очолював уряд і гарно заробляв. За його словами, він має понад €250 тисяч, які отримав від медіа за рішеннями судів у справах про захист честі й репутації. Проте, як зазначають журналісти, цю цифру у €250 тисяч Фіцо регулярно згадує ще з 2012 року, відповідаючи на запитання журналістів про походження грошей, на які він купує елітне житло чи орендує приватні літаки. Ім'я Катаріни Салайової вперше пов’язали з Робертом Фіцо в червні 2020 року. Тоді журналісти помітили, як вони разом приїжджали до братиславського готелю DoubleTree by Hilton, а вранці залишали його окремо. На той момент Фіцо вже був колишнім прем'єр-міністром і очолював парламентську опозицію, а Салайова проходила стажування в Братиславській обласній прокуратурі. ЗМІ дізналися, що вона молодша за премʼєра приблизно на 25—26 років, тобто зараз Салайовій приблизно 35 років. Журналісти також з’ясували, що вона користувалася житлом в одному з найдорожчих районів Братислави — у комплексі мільйонерів River Park на набережній Дунаю. Журналісти поставили під сумнів обставини працевлаштування Салайової до прокуратури. Наприкінці 2018 року вона взяла участь у конкурсі серед 375 претендентів, отримала 95 зі 100 можливих балів і посіла сьоме місце. Завдяки високому результату дівчина могла самостійно обрати місце стажування. Вона зупинилася на прокуратурі Братислави, яку на той час очолював Светозар Хабада — чоловік сестри Роберта Фіцо. Коли словацькі медіа вибухнули повідомленнями про ймовірну коханку Фіцо, про стосунки з нею запитали самого премʼєра та сказали, що бачили його із молодою жінкою. «А з ким мені зустрічатися? З молодими хлопцями?» — відповів Фіцо. Напередодні Різдва 2023 року, невдовзі після повернення до влади, Роберт Фіцо придбав квартиру в Братиславі за 509 тисяч євро у депутата його ж партії. За словами Киселя, премʼєр не оформлював іпотеку для купівлі житла, однак досі не пояснив походження коштів. Помешкання площею близько 129 кв. м розташоване на останньому поверсі житлового комплексу Sokolská Residence, а площа його тераси перевищує 186 кв. м. Експерти ринку нерухомості оцінюють квартиру щонайменше у 850 тисяч євро — значно більше за суму, яку назвав Фіцо. Сам прем'єр Словаччини стверджував, що йдеться про «звичайну трикімнатну квартиру» в будинку, де мешкають молоді родини, та дорікав журналістам за їхні запитання. У серпні 2025 року журналісти помітили Фіцо у новому будинку на схилі над морем, який продавався приблизно за €1,19 мільйона у хорватському місті Ряжань. У Фіцо поцікавилися, кому належить будинок, на що він сказав «відчепитися від нього на відпочинку».
